pr.title: Manually invalidate caches in SimplifyCfg.
pr.description:
The current `SimplifyCfg` pass unconditionally invalidates CFG caches. This is unfortunate if there are no modifications that require this invalidation.

classification.name: SimplifyCfg
evidence: shared implementation file: compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/simplify.rs; name present in diff

processing.reason: PR #142542 is a cache-invalidation performance optimization, not a semantic bug fix. The pre-PR code unconditionally invalidated CFG caches by using `body.basic_blocks_mut()`. The post-PR code preserves caches during `CfgSimplifier` construction and invalidates them only when `simplify()` reports an actual CFG change; `remove_dead_blocks` still uses `body.basic_blocks.as_mut()`, which invalidates caches itself. I inspected the historical `simplify.rs` and `basic_blocks.rs`: every CFG-affecting operation in `simplify` (`collapse_goto_chain`, `simplify_branch`, `merge_successor`) sets the tracked `changed` flag, while `strip_nops` only changes statements and does not affect any cached CFG property. Thus there is no concrete Rust input for which the historical unconditional invalidation and the new conditional invalidation produce different observable values, and the supplied patch contains no regression test or MIR semantic diff. Constructing a source pair that differs would require fabricating a stale-cache bug or an untracked CFG mutation that the actual patch does not contain, which would be an unrelated rewrite rather than the historical transformation.

analysis.summary: SimplifyCfg cache-invalidation optimization: avoid invalidating MIR CFG caches when CfgSimplifier makes no CFG change, and propagate a changed flag so the caller invalidates only after actual simplification.
analysis.originalLogic: `simplify_cfg` called `CfgSimplifier::new(tcx, body).simplify()` unconditionally, and `CfgSimplifier::new` obtained blocks via `body.basic_blocks_mut()`. The PR states: "The current `SimplifyCfg` pass unconditionally invalidates CFG caches. This is unfortunate if there are no modifications that require this invalidation." `simplify` previously returned nothing (`fn simplify(mut self)`), so the caller could not know whether the CFG had changed.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical implementation unconditionally used the cache-invalidating mutable accessor (`body.basic_blocks_mut()`) at CfgSimplifier construction, even when the simplification loop made no modifications. The corrected transformation uses `body.basic_blocks.as_mut_preserves_cfg()` ("Do not clear caches yet. The caller to `simplify` will do it if anything changed."), makes `simplify` return `bool` with `#[must_use]`, tracks whether any outer loop iteration changed, and only then calls `body.basic_blocks.invalidate_cfg_cache()` in `simplify_cfg`.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR bodies passed to the `SimplifyCfg` pass. The relevant distinction is whether `CfgSimplifier` actually performs CFG simplifications: bodies whose loop finds no `changed` iteration (no needed cache invalidation) versus bodies where at least one iteration changes the CFG. Statement-only changes such as `strip_nops` are distinct from the CFG modification tracked by the returned flag.
analysis.trigger: Running `SimplifyCfg` on a MIR body for which the CfgSimplifier fixpoint loop performs no CFG-changing simplification, while caches are still valid.
preconditions: The body is being processed by `simplify_cfg`/`CfgSimplifier`.
CFG caches may be present and valid before the pass.
Any actual CFG modification requires cache invalidation before caches are read again.
pitfalls: Using `as_mut_preserves_cfg()` (or otherwise suppressing invalidation) without invalidating on an actual CFG change leaves stale CFG caches inconsistent with the modified CFG.
The changed flag must cover every iteration of the outer simplification loop: `outer_changed` is set whenever `changed` is true before the loop repeats.
Do not conflate statement cleanup such as `strip_nops()` with CFG topology changes; the returned flag in this patch is driven by the simplification loop's `changed` state.
The caller must consume the `#[must_use]` return value and perform invalidation itself, because construction deliberately no longer clears caches.
analysis.testStrategy: Compare two MIR bodies that differ only in whether `CfgSimplifier` makes a CFG change: one requiring no simplification and one with a mergeable/removable CFG pattern. Verify that no-change cases avoid cache invalidation while changed cases invalidate and that subsequent CFG-cache queries reflect the rewritten CFG. The supplied patch contains no regression-test changes; the post-patch read layer reports an empty MIR diff section, so no test execution or reproduction is claimed.
evidence: The current `SimplifyCfg` pass unconditionally invalidates CFG caches. This is unfortunate if there are no modifications that require this invalidation.
+        // Do not clear caches yet. The caller to `simplify` will do it if anything changed.
